I used to be a carpenter.

If you're looking into post-collapse kind of stuff then that's a whole different thing. The vast majority of carpenters I've known (including myself) would be almost completely lost without power tools.

I think one of the reasons that woodworking has become dominated by cheaply made un-repairable Ikea shit is because of power tools and more advanced woodworking tools like CNC machines. A fully equipped shop can go from rough hewn wood to a brand new bookshelf in less than a day. It wouldn't just be one bookshelf (or whatever really) it would be several because of the assembly line like production capabilities.

If you have to hand plane, square, mould, shape, sand and stain all of that by hand it dramatically increases the production time and with it the cost of the item. With the increased cost people expect it to last and to be a little nicer than the cheap Ikea shit.

I used to go onto custom woodworking sites to see how much one-of-a-kind items that I knew I could build were going for. A coffee table like the one I have in my living room would go for several hundred dollars. Its nearly solid mahogany, just the top is veneered MDF. I made it for free (out of shop scrap) and payed someone $20 to stain it eight years ago.

Back to the point if its post-collapse you're worried about then learn how to use hand-tools instead of power tools. If that's not your concern then just get some tools together and start building stuff, that's the only way to really learn. There are also a ton of YouTube videos out there and if you have any questions feel free to PM me.
